Most of the structures are temporary and are dismantled after the fair closes, except for landmark towers. By far the most famous of these is the [Eiffel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower "Eiffel Tower"), built for the [Exposition Universelle (1889)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1889) "Exposition Universelle (1889)"). Although it is now the most recognized symbol of its host city [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), there were contemporary critics opposed to its construction, and demands for it to be dismantled after the fair's conclusion.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair#cite_note-23)

Other structures that remain from these fairs:

*   1851 – London: [The Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace"), from the first World's Fair in London, designed so that it could be recycled to recoup losses, was such a success that it was moved and intended to be permanent, only to be destroyed by a fire in 1936.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair#cite_note-burning-24)
*   1876 – Philadelphia: The [Centennial Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Exposition "Centennial Exposition")'s main building, [Memorial Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Hall_(Philadelphia) "Memorial Hall (Philadelphia)"), is still in [Fairmount Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairmount_Park "Fairmount Park"), [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and serving as the new home for the [Please Touch Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Please_Touch_Museum "Please Touch Museum"). The space under the entrance to [Memorial Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Hall_(Philadelphia) "Memorial Hall (Philadelphia)") houses a scale model of the entire Exposition.
*   1880 – Melbourne: The [World Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site")–listed [Royal Exhibition Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Exhibition_Building "Royal Exhibition Building") in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), constructed for the [Melbourne International Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_International_Exhibition_(1880) "Melbourne International Exhibition (1880)").
*   1893 – Chicago: The [Museum of Science and Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Science_and_Industry_(Chicago) "Museum of Science and Industry (Chicago)") in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") is housed in the former Palace of Fine Arts, one of the last remaining buildings of the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition"). In conjunction with the fair, the [Art Institute of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Institute_of_Chicago "Art Institute of Chicago") building was built to house conferences, as the World's Congress Auxiliary Building. The [Garden of the Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_of_the_Phoenix "Garden of the Phoenix"), a remnant of the Japanese pavilion, also survives. The intent or hope was to make all Columbian structures permanent, but most of the structures burned, possibly the result of arson during the [Pullman Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pullman_Strike "Pullman Strike"). The foundation of the world's first [Ferris Wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferris_Wheel_(1893) "Ferris Wheel (1893)"), which operated at the Exposition, was unearthed on the [Chicago Midway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Plaisance "Midway Plaisance") during a construction project by [the University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"), whose campus now surrounds the Midway. Relocated survivors include the Norway pavilion, a small house now at a museum in Wisconsin, and the Maine State Building, now at the Poland Springs Resort in Maine.
*   1894 – San Francisco: The [Japanese Tea Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Tea_Garden_(San_Francisco,_California) "Japanese Tea Garden (San Francisco, California)") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco")'s [Golden Gate Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate_Park "Golden Gate Park") is the last major remnant of the [California Midwinter International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Midwinter_International_Exposition_of_1894 "California Midwinter International Exposition of 1894"). Large ornamental wooden gates and a pagoda from the 1915 [Panama–Pacific International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama%E2%80%93Pacific_International_Exposition "Panama–Pacific International Exposition") were brought in after the latter fair closed,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair#cite_note-25) making the Tea Garden a rare if not unique instance of a survivor that incorporates architectural features from two completely separate fairs.
*   1897 – Nashville: A full-scale replica of the [Parthenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon_(Nashville) "Parthenon (Nashville)") was built for the [Tennessee Centennial and International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Centennial_and_International_Exposition "Tennessee Centennial and International Exposition") where it stands today in [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville "Nashville")'s [Centennial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Park_(Nashville) "Centennial Park (Nashville)"). It features plaster reproductions of the [Elgin Marbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elgin_Marbles "Elgin Marbles") and, in 1990, a re-creation of the original [Athena Parthenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athena_Parthenos "Athena Parthenos") statue was installed inside just as it was in the original [Parthenon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon "Parthenon") in ancient Greece.
*   1900 – Paris: the [Grand Palais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Palais "Grand Palais") and [Petit Palais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit_Palais "Petit Palais").
*   [![Image 113](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/1904_World%27s_Fair_Administration_Building_%28Brookings_Hall%2C_Washington_University%29_seen_from_the_southeast_with_the_Italian_Pavilion_in_the_foreground.jpg/250px-1904_World%27s_Fair_Administration_Building_%28Brookings_Hall%2C_Washington_University%29_seen_from_the_southeast_with_the_Italian_Pavilion_in_the_foreground.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1904_World's_Fair_Administration_Building_(Brookings_Hall,_Washington_University)_seen_from_the_southeast_with_the_Italian_Pavilion_in_the_foreground.jpg)

[Brookings Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Hall "Brookings Hall") at [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis"), the administration building of the [1904 World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition "Louisiana Purchase Exposition")

1904 – St. Louis: The [St. Louis Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Art_Museum "St. Louis Art Museum") in [Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Park_(St._Louis,_Missouri) "Forest Park (St. Louis, Missouri)"), originally the Palace of the Fine Arts, and [Brookings Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Hall "Brookings Hall") at [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis"), are remnants of the [Louisiana Purchase Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition "Louisiana Purchase Exposition") (held a year late, as it was originally intended to be the centennial of the [Louisiana Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase "Louisiana Purchase"). But organizers, and President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt"), wanted the fair to be held during the Olympics which were moved from Chicago.), better known as the St. Louis World's Fair. The aviary in Forest Park gave root to the [St. Louis Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Zoo "St. Louis Zoo").
*   1906 – Milan: The [Civic Aquarium of Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Aquarium_of_Milan "Civic Aquarium of Milan") built for the [Milan Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan_International_(1906) "Milan International (1906)") is still open after 100 years and was recently renovated. The [International Commission on Occupational Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Commission_on_Occupational_Health "International Commission on Occupational Health") (ICOH) was settled in Milan during the fair and had its first congress in the Expo pavilions. In June 2006 the ICOH celebrated the first century of its life in Milan. An elevated railway with trains running at short intervals linked the fair to the city center. It was dismantled in the 1920s.
*   1909 – Seattle: The landscaping (by the Olmsted brothers) from the [Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska%E2%80%93Yukon%E2%80%93Pacific_Exposition "Alaska–Yukon–Pacific Exposition") (AYPE) in Seattle still forms much of the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") campus. The only major building left from the AYPE, Architecture Hall, is used by the university's architecture school.
*   1915 – San Francisco: The [Palace of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Fine_Arts "Palace of Fine Arts") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") and its adjacent artificial lagoon are the only major remnants of the [Panama–Pacific International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama%E2%80%93Pacific_International_Exposition "Panama–Pacific International Exposition") still in their original locations on the former fairgrounds (now the city's [Marina District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marina_District,_San_Francisco "Marina District, San Francisco") neighborhood), but the building is almost entirely a reconstruction. The plaster-surfaced original, not intended to survive after the fair, was a crumbling ruin in 1964 when all but the steel framework was demolished so that it could be reproduced in concrete. The San Francisco Civic Auditorium, now the [Bill Graham Civic Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Graham_Civic_Auditorium "Bill Graham Civic Auditorium"), is another major legacy of the fair but was built off-site in the city's [Civic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Center,_San_Francisco "Civic Center, San Francisco"). The independent [Panama–California Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama%E2%80%93California_Exposition "Panama–California Exposition") in [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego") left a substantial legacy of permanent buildings and other structures which today define its site, San Diego's central [Balboa Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balboa_Park_(San_Diego) "Balboa Park (San Diego)"), including the Prado walkway, the California Tower and Dome (now home to the [Museum of Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Museum_of_Us "San Diego Museum of Us")), the 1,500-foot Cabrillo Bridge, the lily pond and botanical gardens, and the [Spreckels Organ Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spreckels_Organ_Pavilion "Spreckels Organ Pavilion").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair#cite_note-26)
*   1929 – Seville and Barcelona: much survives from the two simultaneous fairs [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") hosted that year. The most famous are the remnants of the [Ibero-American Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibero-American_Exposition_of_1929 "Ibero-American Exposition of 1929") in [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville"), in which the Spanish Pavilion's _Plaza de España_ forms part of a large park and forecourt. Most of that fair's pavilions have survived and been adapted for other uses, with many of them becoming [consulates-general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulate-general "Consulate-general") for the countries that built them. The [Barcelona International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1929_Barcelona_International_Exposition "1929 Barcelona International Exposition") featured the famous [German pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Pavilion "Barcelona Pavilion") designed by [Mies van der Rohe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mies_van_der_Rohe "Mies van der Rohe"), which was demolished but later rebuilt on the original site.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair#cite_note-27)
*   1936 – Johannesburg: The [Empire Exhibition, South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_Exhibition,_South_Africa "Empire Exhibition, South Africa") was built close to the [University of the Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand "University of the Witwatersrand"), and by the late 1970s the growth of the university was large enough to incorporate the permanent buildings from the exhibition. In 1985, the university purchased the South African Government Building; the two Heavy Machinery Halls, now called Empire Hall and the Dining Hall; the Hall of Transport; the Tower of Light; the Cape Dutch complex; and the Bien Donne Restaurant.
*   1939 – New York City: [The New York City Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens_Museum "Queens Museum") from the [1939's World Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_New_York_World's_Fair "1939 New York World's Fair"), was reused for the 1964 World's Fair and is now the Queens Museum. [Parachute jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute_jump "Parachute jump") was a ride from the fair. It was moved to the [Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island "Coney Island") boardwalk in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   1942 – Rome: A special case is the [EUR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esposizione_Universale_Roma "Esposizione Universale Roma") quarter in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), built for a World's Fair planned for 1942 but cancelled because of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Today it hosts governmental and private offices, and several museums.
*   1958 – Brussels: In [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), the [Atomium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomium "Atomium") still stands at the exposition site. It is a 165-billion-times-enlarged iron-crystal-shaped building. Until June 2012, the "American Theatre" on the Expo grounds was frequently used as a television studio by the [VRT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlaamse_Radio-_en_Televisieomroeporganisatie "Vlaamse Radio- en Televisieomroeporganisatie").

*   1962 – Seattle: The [Space Needle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Needle "Space Needle") theme building of the [Century 21 Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Century_21_Exposition "Century 21 Exposition") commonly known as the Seattle World's Fair still stands as a [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") icon and landmark. The [Seattle Center Monorail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Center_Monorail "Seattle Center Monorail"), the other widely known futuristic feature of the fair, still operates daily. The US pavilion became the [Pacific Science Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Science_Center "Pacific Science Center"). The original exterior and roof of the Washington State Pavilion has been preserved as a landmark, and now is part of [Climate Pledge Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Pledge_Arena "Climate Pledge Arena").

[![Image 115](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Unisphere-2_%2827835155267%29.jpg/250px-Unisphere-2_%2827835155267%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Unisphere-2_(27835155267).jpg)

The Unisphere, from the 1964 World's Fair in New York City, in the 21st century

*   1964 – New York City: many structures still stand 
    *   The [Unisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unisphere "Unisphere"), built for the [second New York World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_New_York_World's_Fair "1964 New York World's Fair"), stands on its original site in Flushing Meadows, Queens
    *   [New York Hall of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Hall_of_Science "New York Hall of Science"), built for the fair, continues to operate as a science museum, similar to its original role
    *   The Port Authority Heliport and Exhibit is now the [Terrace on the Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrace_on_the_Park "Terrace on the Park") event and catering venue
    *   The [New York State Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Pavilion "New York State Pavilion") is mostly derelict, but is still an icon, with its observation towers prominently featured in 1997's _[Men in Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men\_in\_Black\_(1997\_film) "Men in Black (1997 film)")_. The Theaterama building is the only portion still maintained, and is used by the [Queens Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens_Theatre_in_the_Park "Queens Theatre in the Park"). The Tent of Tomorrow building and observation towers are being restored as of 2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=World%27s_fair&action=edit).
    *   The New York City Pavilion, a holdover from the [1939 fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_New_York_World's_Fair "1939 New York World's Fair"), continues to serve as the home of the [Queens Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens_Museum "Queens Museum")
    *   Other artifacts remain throughout the park, and many buildings were transported for use elsewhere and continue to function.

*   1967 – Montreal: Among [the structures still standing from Expo 67 in Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_67_pavilions#Extant_pavilions "Expo 67 pavilions") are [Moshe Safdie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshe_Safdie "Moshe Safdie")'s [Habitat 67](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitat_67 "Habitat 67"), [Buckminster Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckminster_Fuller "Buckminster Fuller")'s American pavilion the "[Montreal Biosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Biosph%C3%A8re "Montreal Biosphère")", the Jamaica Pavilion, the Tunisia Pavilion, and the French pavilion (now the [Montreal Casino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Casino "Montreal Casino")).
*   1968 – San Antonio: San Antonio kept the [Tower of the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_the_Americas "Tower of the Americas") and the Convention Center from HemisFair '68.
*   1970 – Osaka: The [Tower of the Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_the_Sun "Tower of the Sun") was left standing, but was neglected after the conclusion of the [Expo '70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'70 "Expo '70"). # About World Expos

World Expos, officially known as International Registered Exhibitions, are a global gathering of nations dedicated to finding solutions to pressing challenges of our time by offering a journey inside a universal theme through engaging and immersive activities. World Expos welcome tens of millions of visitors, allow countries to build extraordinary pavilions and transform the host city for years to come.

The first World Expo – the Great Exhibition – took place in London in 1851. The concept became popular and was repeated across the globe, demonstrating an unparalleled power of attraction and a record of world-class legacies. Since the BIE was created in 1928 to regulate and oversee these mega-events, World Expos have explicitly been organised around a theme that attempts to improve humankind’s knowledge, takes into account human and social aspirations and highlights scientific, technological, economic and social progress.

In the modern era, World Expos are unrivalled among international events in their size, scale, duration and visitor numbers. They are large-scale platforms for education and progress that serve as a bridge between governments, companies, international organisations, and citizens.

The most recent World Expo - Expo 2025 Osaka Kansai - was organised in Japan under the theme “Designing Future Society for Our Lives”, and welcomed over 29 million visitors.

The next World Expo, Expo 2030 Riyadh, will take place in Saudi Arabia between 1 October 2030 and 31 March 2031 under the theme "Foresight for Tomorrow".

View the full list of [all World Expos](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/en/expo-index/all-world-expos) since 1851

| --- |
| Official Designation | International Registered Exhibition* |
| Organiser | Host country |
| Theme | A universal challenge of our time |
| Duration | Up to six months |
| Frequency | Every five years** |
| Size | No maximum size (Expo 2020 Dubai covered 438 ha) |
| Pavilions | Participants may build their own pavilions or rent a dedicated space*** |
| Official Participants | Countries and International Organisations |
| Non-Official Participants | Cities, Regions, Companies, Civil Society and NGOs |

* The 1928 Paris Convention initially referred to ‘General Exhibitions of the 1st category’ and ‘General Exhibitions of the 2nd category’. Following a protocol to the Convention in 1972, the two categories were replaced by a single classification ‘World Exhibition’. A new amendment adopted in 1988 and applied from 1996 gave World Expos their current official term ‘International Registered Exhibition’.

** The interval between two World Expos has differed through time. The 1928 convention fixed a minimum of six years between two World Expos of the same category (with some exceptions introduced in its 1948 Protocol). The 1972 Protocol introduced an interval of 10 years, and the 1988 Protocol fixed the current interval to 5 years.

***‘The difference between General Exhibitions of the 1st and 2nd category was that in the latter, participants could not be induced to construct their own pavilions.

# About World Expos

World Expos, officially known as International Registered Exhibitions, are a global gathering of nations dedicated to finding solutions to pressing challenges of our time by offering a journey inside a universal theme through engaging and immersive activities. World Expos welcome tens of millions of visitors, allow countries to build extraordinary pavilions and transform the host city for years to come.

The first World Expo – the Great Exhibition – took place in London in 1851. The concept became popular and was repeated across the globe, demonstrating an unparalleled power of attraction and a record of world-class legacies. Since the BIE was created in 1928 to regulate and oversee these mega-events, World Expos have explicitly been organised around a theme that attempts to improve humankind’s knowledge, takes into account human and social aspirations and highlights scientific, technological, economic and social progress.

In the modern era, World Expos are unrivalled among international events in their size, scale, duration and visitor numbers. They are large-scale platforms for education and progress that serve as a bridge between governments, companies, international organisations, and citizens.

The most recent World Expo - Expo 2025 Osaka Kansai - was organised in Japan under the theme “Designing Future Society for Our Lives”, and welcomed over 29 million visitors.

The next World Expo, Expo 2030 Riyadh, will take place in Saudi Arabia between 1 October 2030 and 31 March 2031 under the theme "Foresight for Tomorrow".

The **Exposição Internacional do Porto**, known in English as the **International Exhibition of 1865**, was a [world's fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair "World's fair") held in the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") city of [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"). The exhibition was housed inside the grand _[Palácio de Cristal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal\_Palace\_(Porto) "Crystal Palace (Porto)")_, which was modelled on the synonymous [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") erected for [The Great Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Exhibition "The Great Exhibition") held during 1851 in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The building's designer was Anglo-Irish civil engineer [Francis Webb Sheilds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Webb_Sheilds "Francis Webb Sheilds"), who also engineered its construction – he had been the resident engineer for the earlier building between 1852 and 1858.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-Wagga_Wagga_Express-2) The building was demolished in 1951 after hosting many other expositions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-3)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1865_International_Exhibition&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The exhibition was inaugurated on 18 September 1865[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-ref01-4) in the presence of the Portuguese king, [Luís I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lu%C3%ADs_I_of_Portugal "Luís I of Portugal") and his consort [Maria Pia of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Pia_of_Savoy "Maria Pia of Savoy"). Upon inauguration, it became the first world's fair to occur on the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). The exhibition was shown until January 1866, and the theme of the event was industrial and trade innovations with an emphasis in primary materials, machinery, manufacture and fine arts.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-5)

## Organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1865_International_Exhibition&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Organization")]

Chiefly organized by the _Associação Industrial Portuense_ (today called the _Associação Empresarial de Portugal_), the exhibition hosted 3,139 exhibitors, of which 499 were [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), 265 [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), 107 [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), 89 [Belgian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), 62 [Brazilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), 24 [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and 16 [Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"). [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") were also represented.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-6)

World's fair in Porto, Portugal, in 1865

The **Exposição Internacional do Porto**, known in English as the **International Exhibition of 1865**, was a [world's fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_fair "World's fair") held in the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") city of [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto "Porto"). The exhibition was housed inside the grand _[Palácio de Cristal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal\_Palace\_(Porto) "Crystal Palace (Porto)")_, which was modelled on the synonymous [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace "The Crystal Palace") erected for [The Great Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Exhibition "The Great Exhibition") held during 1851 in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). The building's designer was Anglo-Irish civil engineer [Francis Webb Sheilds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Webb_Sheilds "Francis Webb Sheilds"), who also engineered its construction – he had been the resident engineer for the earlier building between 1852 and 1858.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-Wagga_Wagga_Express-2) The building was demolished in 1951 after hosting many other expositions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-3)

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1865_International_Exhibition&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The exhibition was inaugurated on 18 September 1865[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-ref01-4) in the presence of the Portuguese king, [Luís I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lu%C3%ADs_I_of_Portugal "Luís I of Portugal") and his consort [Maria Pia of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Pia_of_Savoy "Maria Pia of Savoy"). Upon inauguration, it became the first world's fair to occur on the [Iberian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula "Iberian Peninsula"). The exhibition was shown until January 1866, and the theme of the event was industrial and trade innovations with an emphasis in primary materials, machinery, manufacture and fine arts.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-5)

## Organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1865_International_Exhibition&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Organization")]

Chiefly organized by the _Associação Industrial Portuense_ (today called the _Associação Empresarial de Portugal_), the exhibition hosted 3,139 exhibitors, of which 499 were [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), 265 [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), 107 [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), 89 [Belgian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), 62 [Brazilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), 24 [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), and 16 [Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark"). [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"), [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") were also represented.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1865_International_Exhibition#cite_note-6)

# World’s Fairs - EXPOs

More than 160 years ago, in 1851, the first world’s fair took place in London. It proved to be a huge success - one that was subsequently repeated by numerous international exhibitions. But with the growing number (and declining success) of these events a sanctioning body became necessary: The Convention Relating to International Exhibitions was adopted in 1928 - with Austria being one of its founding member states.

The Bureau International des Expositions or BIE (International Exhibitions Bureau) was established in Paris to manage this Convention, with membership open to all countries. Currently the BIE counts 170 member states, among them Austria, with the Federal Ministry for Digital and Economic Affairs as the lead.

## What kinds of World’s Fairs are there?

The Convention distinguishes two categories of EXPOs:

*   'International Registered Exhibitions' or 'World EXPOs': These large-scale events focusing on a universal topic take place every five years, lasting up to six months. The size of the exhibition area is not limited by the Convention.
*   'International Recognized Exhibitions' or 'Specialized EXPOs': These events have a more narrowly defined theme, last no more than three months and have a limited size of the exhibition area of a maximum of 25 hectares.

Austria has participated in the vast majority of EXPOs, hosting once in 1873 in Vienna (theme “Culture and Education).

## Current World’s Fair

### EXPO 2025 Osaka-Kansai

The current EXPO takes place in Osaka, Japan from April 13th to October 13th, 2025 with the motto “Designing Future Society for Our Lives”. The site is located on the man-made island of Yumeshima, 10 kilometers from Osaka city center. It is the second time since 1970 that an EXPO has been held in Osaka.

![Image 2](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:3f252379-4d17-4ebb-ade6-81f22f8c80e8/Au%C3%9Fenansicht_Pavillon_EXPO_Osaka.jpg)

 photo: Expo Austria/BWM Designers & Architects 

A total of over 28 million visitors and more than 160 participating countries as well as 25 international organizations are expected.

#### The Austrian pavilion – “Composing the Future”

Music is a connecting element of Austrian and Japanese culture. Classical music from Austria is particularly popular in Japan. The Austrian pavilion interprets the motto of the Expo in Osaka – “Designing Future Society for Our Lives” – musically. The future is composed in Austria: “Composing the Future”.

![Image 3](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:55da8b51-0196-4727-a27c-995aebbd9a9c/bf3cc893f9383ec44b2d18e7cd4857f7.png)

 photo: Expo Austria/BWM Designers & Architects 

The exhibition rooms show Austria's contributions to a future worth living. Based on the diversity of the relationships between Austria and Japan, visitors can experience the diversity of the Austrian economy and society through people and ideas.

[More about the Expo 2025 Osaka](https://www.expoaustria.at/en/ "Opens in a new Tab")

## Most recent World’s Fairs

More than 60 World’s Fairs have taken place to date, the most recent ones in Aichi/Japan 2005, Zaragoza/Spain 2008, Shanghai/PRC 2010, Yeosu/South Korea 2012, Milan/Italy 2015, Astana/Kazakhstan 2017 and Dubai 2020.

### EXPO 2020 Dubai

Dubai, the largest city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), hosted a registered World EXPO from October 2021 to April 2022. The motto 'Connecting Minds, Creating the Future' was divided into three sub-themes: Opportunity, Mobility and Sustainability. EXPO Dubai was the first world’s fair held in the MENA (Middle East Northern Africa) region.

The UAE are Austria’s most important trading partner in the region with Dubai especially serving as a hub for Austrian companies. Austria has announced its participation in 2017, funded and organized, as in the past, by the Federal Ministry Labour and Economy together with the Austrian Federal Economic Chambers. Austria build its own pavilion, located in the “Opportunity” district, between the pavilions of Switzerland and China.

![Image 4: Der Österreich-Pavillon von außen](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:f13a8179-9ab5-462d-80e8-2452424e0526/%C3%96sterreich_Pavillon_au%C3%9Fen.jpg)

 The Austrian pavilion "in dialogue with austria"; ©Querkraft Architekten 

The Austrian pavilion combined Arabic building traditions with Austrian know-how, joining the advantages of high- and low-tech solutions. The result was a pavilion with significantly lower energy needs due to natural cooling. The architecture also provided an interesting backdrop to the exhibition within the pavilion, showcasing Austria as a world leader in digitalization, high-tech, science and research.

The Austrian pavilion also offered Austrian hospitality, coffee and sweets at a traditional Kaffeehaus.

Throughout the six months of EXPO Dubai, economic and cultural events accompanied Austria’s participation. The highlight was the Austrian National Day, which took place on November 18, 2021.

### EXPO 2017 Astana

The Kazakh capital Astana (since renamed Nur-Sultan) hosted a specialized EXPO on the theme 'Future Energy' from June to September of 2017. 115 countries and 22 international organizations participated, with more than 3.8 million visitors.

![Image 5: Ausstellungsgelände](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:34e048f4-20ce-4342-872e-1f34ed5a78f4/Ausstellungsgelaende.jpg)

The area of EXPO 2017 Astana; © EXPO Astana photo: EXPO Astana 

Austria interpreted the theme with a contribution entitled 'With brain, heart and muscle power – The Austrian Power machine'. In a hall, shared with the Czech Republic, Luxembourg, Latvia, Greece and Switzerland, Austria presented its topic on 900 m² in a playful manner. The presentation won the iF Design Award and the Red Dot Award for innovative design.

![Image 6: Austrian Power Machine bunt](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:239df784-fb45-44e8-a975-bbab0fe7e828/05.jpg)

“The Austrian Power Machine”; © expoaustria photo: expoaustria 

But Austria was present at EXPO Astana in other ways as well: four out of only 23 award-winning projects at the 'Energy Best Practice Area' were from Austria, and three Austrian companies were involved in the construction of the EXPO grounds.

### EXPO 2015 Milan

Milan was host of a World Exhibition taking place from May to October 2015 with the motto 'Feeding the Planet, Energy for Life'.

Austria interpreted this theme by putting the most important food into focus: air. Titled 'breathe.austria', the Austrian pavilion showcased a forest ecosystem including around 12,000 trees and plants.

This ecosystem not only lowered the temperature within the pavilion without air conditioning but also generated oxygen for 1,800 people per hour. Rooftop photovoltaic panels made the Austrian pavilion energy-neutral - meaning it produced more electricity than it needed.

![Image 7: Der österreichische Beitrag "breathe.austria" auf der EXPO Milano 2015](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:d2001ff6-9235-42cb-84d6-ee94897e56e0/BreatheAustria.jpg)

Inside the Austrian pavilion; © expoaustria photo: ARTWORK COMPANY 

The public was wowed by this concept: more than 2.4 million visitors went to see the Austrian pavilion, sometimes queuing for hours. The pavilion was also awarded several prizes, among them awards by the EXPO organizer and the Italian Ministry of the Environment.

# World’s Fairs - EXPOs

More than 160 years ago, in 1851, the first world’s fair took place in London. It proved to be a huge success - one that was subsequently repeated by numerous international exhibitions. But with the growing number (and declining success) of these events a sanctioning body became necessary: The Convention Relating to International Exhibitions was adopted in 1928 - with Austria being one of its founding member states.

The Bureau International des Expositions or BIE (International Exhibitions Bureau) was established in Paris to manage this Convention, with membership open to all countries. Currently the BIE counts 170 member states, among them Austria, with the Federal Ministry for Digital and Economic Affairs as the lead.

## What kinds of World’s Fairs are there?

The Convention distinguishes two categories of EXPOs:

*   'International Registered Exhibitions' or 'World EXPOs': These large-scale events focusing on a universal topic take place every five years, lasting up to six months. The size of the exhibition area is not limited by the Convention.
*   'International Recognized Exhibitions' or 'Specialized EXPOs': These events have a more narrowly defined theme, last no more than three months and have a limited size of the exhibition area of a maximum of 25 hectares.

Austria has participated in the vast majority of EXPOs, hosting once in 1873 in Vienna (theme “Culture and Education).

## Current World’s Fair

### EXPO 2025 Osaka-Kansai

The current EXPO takes place in Osaka, Japan from April 13th to October 13th, 2025 with the motto “Designing Future Society for Our Lives”. The site is located on the man-made island of Yumeshima, 10 kilometers from Osaka city center. It is the second time since 1970 that an EXPO has been held in Osaka.

![Image 2](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:3f252379-4d17-4ebb-ade6-81f22f8c80e8/Au%C3%9Fenansicht_Pavillon_EXPO_Osaka.jpg)

 photo: Expo Austria/BWM Designers & Architects 

A total of over 28 million visitors and more than 160 participating countries as well as 25 international organizations are expected.

#### The Austrian pavilion – “Composing the Future”

Music is a connecting element of Austrian and Japanese culture. Classical music from Austria is particularly popular in Japan. The Austrian pavilion interprets the motto of the Expo in Osaka – “Designing Future Society for Our Lives” – musically. The future is composed in Austria: “Composing the Future”.

![Image 3](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:55da8b51-0196-4727-a27c-995aebbd9a9c/bf3cc893f9383ec44b2d18e7cd4857f7.png)

 photo: Expo Austria/BWM Designers & Architects 

The exhibition rooms show Austria's contributions to a future worth living. Based on the diversity of the relationships between Austria and Japan, visitors can experience the diversity of the Austrian economy and society through people and ideas.

[More about the Expo 2025 Osaka](https://www.expoaustria.at/en/ "Opens in a new Tab")

## Most recent World’s Fairs

More than 60 World’s Fairs have taken place to date, the most recent ones in Aichi/Japan 2005, Zaragoza/Spain 2008, Shanghai/PRC 2010, Yeosu/South Korea 2012, Milan/Italy 2015, Astana/Kazakhstan 2017 and Dubai 2020.

### EXPO 2020 Dubai

Dubai, the largest city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), hosted a registered World EXPO from October 2021 to April 2022. The motto 'Connecting Minds, Creating the Future' was divided into three sub-themes: Opportunity, Mobility and Sustainability. EXPO Dubai was the first world’s fair held in the MENA (Middle East Northern Africa) region.

The UAE are Austria’s most important trading partner in the region with Dubai especially serving as a hub for Austrian companies. Austria has announced its participation in 2017, funded and organized, as in the past, by the Federal Ministry Labour and Economy together with the Austrian Federal Economic Chambers. Austria build its own pavilion, located in the “Opportunity” district, between the pavilions of Switzerland and China.

![Image 4: Der Österreich-Pavillon von außen](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:f13a8179-9ab5-462d-80e8-2452424e0526/%C3%96sterreich_Pavillon_au%C3%9Fen.jpg)

 The Austrian pavilion "in dialogue with austria"; ©Querkraft Architekten 

The Austrian pavilion combined Arabic building traditions with Austrian know-how, joining the advantages of high- and low-tech solutions. The result was a pavilion with significantly lower energy needs due to natural cooling. The architecture also provided an interesting backdrop to the exhibition within the pavilion, showcasing Austria as a world leader in digitalization, high-tech, science and research.

The Austrian pavilion also offered Austrian hospitality, coffee and sweets at a traditional Kaffeehaus.

Throughout the six months of EXPO Dubai, economic and cultural events accompanied Austria’s participation. The highlight was the Austrian National Day, which took place on November 18, 2021.

### EXPO 2017 Astana

The Kazakh capital Astana (since renamed Nur-Sultan) hosted a specialized EXPO on the theme 'Future Energy' from June to September of 2017. 115 countries and 22 international organizations participated, with more than 3.8 million visitors.

![Image 5: Ausstellungsgelände](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:34e048f4-20ce-4342-872e-1f34ed5a78f4/Ausstellungsgelaende.jpg)

The area of EXPO 2017 Astana; © EXPO Astana photo: EXPO Astana 

Austria interpreted the theme with a contribution entitled 'With brain, heart and muscle power – The Austrian Power machine'. In a hall, shared with the Czech Republic, Luxembourg, Latvia, Greece and Switzerland, Austria presented its topic on 900 m² in a playful manner. The presentation won the iF Design Award and the Red Dot Award for innovative design.

![Image 6: Austrian Power Machine bunt](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:239df784-fb45-44e8-a975-bbab0fe7e828/05.jpg)

“The Austrian Power Machine”; © expoaustria photo: expoaustria 

But Austria was present at EXPO Astana in other ways as well: four out of only 23 award-winning projects at the 'Energy Best Practice Area' were from Austria, and three Austrian companies were involved in the construction of the EXPO grounds.

### EXPO 2015 Milan

Milan was host of a World Exhibition taking place from May to October 2015 with the motto 'Feeding the Planet, Energy for Life'.

Austria interpreted this theme by putting the most important food into focus: air. Titled 'breathe.austria', the Austrian pavilion showcased a forest ecosystem including around 12,000 trees and plants.

This ecosystem not only lowered the temperature within the pavilion without air conditioning but also generated oxygen for 1,800 people per hour. Rooftop photovoltaic panels made the Austrian pavilion energy-neutral - meaning it produced more electricity than it needed.

![Image 7: Der österreichische Beitrag "breathe.austria" auf der EXPO Milano 2015](https://www.bmwet.gv.at/dam/jcr:d2001ff6-9235-42cb-84d6-ee94897e56e0/BreatheAustria.jpg)

Inside the Austrian pavilion; © expoaustria photo: ARTWORK COMPANY 

The public was wowed by this concept: more than 2.4 million visitors went to see the Austrian pavilion, sometimes queuing for hours. The pavilion was also awarded several prizes, among them awards by the EXPO organizer and the Italian Ministry of the Environment.

*   What is a world’s fair?  

A world's fair is a large international exhibition of industrial, scientific, and cultural items from many countries, displayed at a specific site for about three to six months. These fairs often include an entertainment area with rides, attractions, food, and beverages.

The modern world's fair era began with Britain's Great Exhibition in London in 1851, showcasing scientific and technological marvels. Between 1880 and World War I, over 40 international expositions occurred worldwide. The [Bureau International des Expositions (BIE)](https://www.bie-paris.org/site/en), established in 1928, governs and regulates these fairs.

Since 1970, fairs have focused on themes like the environment. Recent expositions have been held in countries such as Japan, China, South Korea, Italy, and Kazakhstan.

*   Where and when was the first world’s fair held?  

The first modern [world's fair](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/world'sfair) was the Great Exhibition, also known as the Crystal Palace Exhibition, which took place in London's Hyde Park in 1851. Organized through the efforts of Prince Albert, it showcased scientific, technological, artistic, and craftsmanship marvels from various countries. The exhibition was housed in the [Crystal Palace](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Crystal-Palace-building-London/Introduction#ref1), an iron-and-glass structure designed by Joseph Paxton. Over six million people attended, and the exhibition made a substantial profit.

*   What are the main purposes of a world’s fair?  

World's fairs serve multiple purposes, including showcasing a wide array of industrial, scientific, and cultural achievements from different countries. They offer entertainment like rides, attractions, and diverse food and beverages.

Since the 1970s, many fairs have shifted focus to enlightening visitors on specific themes, often related to environmental issues, rather than commemorating historical events. Some critics view world’s fairs as extravagant; others believe they remain valuable by addressing social and environmental problems. These events are governed and regulated by the [Bureau International des Expositions (BIE)](https://www.britannica.com/topic/worlds-fair/Introduction#ref1), ensuring proper scheduling and clarifying the rights of host cities and participants.

*   How are different countries represented at a world’s fair?  

At a [world's fair](https://www.britannica.com/topic/worlds-fair/Introduction#ref1), countries are typically represented through national pavilions and exhibits showcasing a wide array of industrial, scientific, and cultural items. These exhibits offer a glimpse into each nation's unique identity and advancements.

For example, the United Kingdom's "Seed Cathedral" at Expo Shanghai 2010 featured tens of thousands of acrylic rods with plant seeds embedded in them. Australia's pavilion evoked the country’s landmark Uluru/Ayers Rock. These displays enable countries to present themselves and their achievements to a global audience.

*   What famous inventions or buildings have been introduced at world’s fairs?  

World's fairs, or international expositions, have been the debut stage for many famous inventions and architectural marvels.

**Buildings**  
 * **The Crystal Palace**, a massive iron-and-glass structure, was built for London’s Great Exhibition of 1851.  
 * The **Eiffel Tower** was constructed for the Paris Exposition of 1889.  
 * The **Trylon and Perisphere** were showcased at the New York World’s Fair of 1939-40.

**Inventions**  
 * The **telephone, typewriter, and mechanical calculator** were introduced at the U.S. Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876.  
 * The **Ferris wheel** debuted at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893.  
 * The **ice cream cone** gained popularity at the St. Louis World’s Fair in 1904.

*   How have world’s fairs changed over time?  

World's fairs have transformed significantly since the first modern fair, the Great Exhibition of 1851. Early fairs showcased industrial, scientific, and cultural items and were a sign of international competition. Between 1880 and World War I, the world's fairs increased in frequency and popularity.

After World War I, fairs declined in cultural status because of improved transportation and communication networks. After 1970, fairs shifted towards specific themes, such as environmental issues and sustainable development, and away from celebrating colonial empires or historical anniversaries.

The fairs of the 21st century have become less frequent because of increasing costs and tighter regulations. Though some critics have called world fairs extravagant and irrelevant, many believe that these fairs can continue to be worthwhile by focusing on social and environmental issues.

**world’s fair**, large [international exhibition](https://www.britannica.com/money/trade-show) of a wide variety of industrial, scientific, and cultural items that are on display at a specific site for a period of time, ranging usually from three to six months. World’s fairs include exhibits from a significant number of countries and often have an entertainment zone in which visitors can enjoy rides, exotic attractions, and food and beverages. Since the mid-19th century more than 100 world’s fairs have been held in more than 20 countries throughout the world. Generally speaking, these events are called world’s fairs in the United States, international (or universal) [expositions](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/expositions) in continental Europe and Asia, and exhibitions in Great Britain. The term _expo_ has also been applied to many expositions in various locations.

World’s fairs are governed and regulated by the Bureau International des Expositions (BIE), a Paris-based organization established in 1928. Its objective is to bring order to exposition scheduling and to make clear the rights and responsibilities of the host city and participants. The original convention that established the BIE and set up guidelines for expositions has been revised a number of times, but as of the early 21st century a large exposition, termed a “registered exhibition,” could be held once every five years, and one smaller exposition, called a “recognized exhibition,” could be held during the interval.

## Early national exhibitions

The English national fairs of the 18th century, which combined trade shows with carnival-like public entertainment, were among the forerunners of the modern world’s fair. In addition, the Society for the Arts (later called the Royal Society for the Arts and, subsequently, the RSA), established in [London](https://www.britannica.com/place/London) in 1754, produced a series of competitive art shows that included industrial arts—various technological [innovations](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/innovations) ranging from spinning wheels to cider presses.

In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the French began hosting industrial exhibitions. These came under the authority of the national government, whose aim was to assist French manufacturers in competing against the British in the international marketplace. The British, confident that their products were superior, never emulated this idea. Instead, the [mechanics’ institutes](https://www.britannica.com/topic/mechanics-institute-British-United-States-organization) in Great Britain began sponsoring exhibitions in the 1830s. These institutes were created to bring scientific [education](https://www.britannica.com/topic/education) to craftsmen and factory workers, and their exhibitions displayed tools and other labour-saving mechanical devices that were based on the latest scientific inventions. The exhibitions of the mechanics’ institutes also featured entertainment and exotic displays, such as so-called “genuine historical relics” of sometimes [dubious](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/dubious) authenticity, as well as fine arts shows that mingled works by local and national artists.

## The Great Exhibition and its legacy: the golden age of fairs

[![Image 22: Crystal Palace](https://cdn.britannica.com/23/18923-050-4BC866A6/transept-Joseph-Paxton-Crystal-Palace-Hyde-Park-1851.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/23/18923-050-4BC866A6/transept-Joseph-Paxton-Crystal-Palace-Hyde-Park-1851.jpg)

[Crystal Palace](https://cdn.britannica.com/23/18923-050-4BC866A6/transept-Joseph-Paxton-Crystal-Palace-Hyde-Park-1851.jpg)Illustration of the transept of the Crystal Palace, designed by Sir Joseph Paxton, at the Great Exhibition of 1851, Hyde Park, London.(more)

The era of the modern world’s fair began with [Britain’s](https://www.britannica.com/place/United-Kingdom)[Great Exhibition](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Great-Exhibition-of-1851) (formally, the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations; often called the [Crystal Palace](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Crystal-Palace-building-London) Exhibition), held in London’s [Hyde Park](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hyde-Park-London) in 1851. It came about through the efforts of [Queen Victoria](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Victoria-queen-of-United-Kingdom)’s husband, [Prince Albert](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Albert-Prince-Consort)—who, because of his Continental background, had a special understanding of the potential value of an exhibition showcasing Britain to an international audience—and through Parliament’s adoption of [free trade](https://www.britannica.com/money/free-trade), which, it was hoped, would lead to more sales of British goods abroad. A royal commission chaired by Prince Albert planned the exhibition and held a competition for a building design. Ultimately, however, the commission rejected all the entries submitted and instead chose a design by [Joseph Paxton](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joseph-Paxton), a greenhouse builder. Paxton’s iron-and-glass structure, dubbed the [Crystal Palace](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Crystal-Palace-building-London), delighted the public and doubtless contributed to the success of the exhibition.

[![Image 23: German political theorist Karl Marx; communism](https://cdn.britannica.com/23/129223-131-ECE7E86C/Karl-Marx.jpg) Britannica Quiz A Study of History: Who, What, Where, and When?](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/a-study-of-history-who-what-where-and-when)
The exhibits on display at the Crystal Palace included scientific and technological marvels from many different countries as well as works of art and craftsmanship. Some six million people attended the exhibition, which earned a substantial profit. (A fund that was created with the profits still provides fellowships to British students in fields such as engineering and industrial design.)

The [legacy](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/legacy) of the Crystal Palace was immense. Its critical and financial success ensured that world’s fairs would continue to be held. The period between 1880 and [World War I](https://www.britannica.com/event/World-War-I) was a golden age of fairs, with more than 40 international expositions held in locations as varied as [Australia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Australia) ([Melbourne](https://www.britannica.com/place/Melbourne), Victoria, 1888; and [Hobart](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hobart-Tasmania-Australia), Tasmania, 1894–95), Guatemala ([Guatemala City](https://www.britannica.com/place/Guatemala-City), 1897), and [Hanoi](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hanoi) (1902–03; then located in [French Indochina](https://www.britannica.com/place/Indochina), now the capital of Vietnam).

In the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-United-States), fairs were inspired by the experience of those who attended and participated in the early fairs in Europe. Although mechanics’ institutes existed in the United States in the 19th century, their occasional exhibitions do not appear to have had much influence on the planners of the earliest American international expositions. One of the very first of these followed in the footsteps of the Great Exhibition. The Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations, more commonly known as the [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City) Crystal Palace Exhibition, was held in 1853–54 in an iron-and-glass structure in Bryant Park. It showcased the same types of displays as its London counterpart but also included an especially impressive sculpture collection. Despite the [fair’s](https://www.britannica.com/money/fair) promise, however, attendance never measured up to expectations, and it ended with a substantial [monetary](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/monetary) loss. It would be more than 20 years before another exposition was held in the United States.

[![Image 27: The Gallery of Machines at the 1889 Universal Exposition, Paris.](https://cdn.britannica.com/29/58629-004-9D67C10B/Gallery-of-Machines-Paris-Universal-Exposition-1889.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/29/58629-004-9D67C10B/Gallery-of-Machines-Paris-Universal-Exposition-1889.jpg)

[The Gallery of Machines at the 1889 Universal Exposition, Paris.](https://cdn.britannica.com/29/58629-004-9D67C10B/Gallery-of-Machines-Paris-Universal-Exposition-1889.jpg)(more)

Not to be outdone by London’s Crystal Palace, fair organizers in [Paris](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paris) held the first in a long series of international expositions in 1855. The exposition occupied a larger space and included exhibits from more countries than the Crystal Palace, and it presented several new features, such as reduced admission prices on Sundays and a separate fine arts pavilion that contained some 5,000 works by artists from 29 countries. Although it lost money, the 1855 Paris exposition left such a positive legacy that the government [sponsored](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/sponsored) subsequent expositions in 1867, 1878, 1889, and 1900, each attracting a larger attendance than the previous one.

[![Image 28: The Horticultural Hall at the U.S. Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, 1876.](https://cdn.britannica.com/07/152607-050-6A886754/Horticultural-Hall-US-Centennial-Exhibition-Philadelphia-1876.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/07/152607-050-6A886754/Horticultural-Hall-US-Centennial-Exhibition-Philadelphia-1876.jpg)

[The Horticultural Hall at the U.S. Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, 1876.](https://cdn.britannica.com/07/152607-050-6A886754/Horticultural-Hall-US-Centennial-Exhibition-Philadelphia-1876.jpg)(more)

By the 1870s the international exposition movement had become sufficiently well established that the planners of the centennial commemoration of [America’s](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-United-States)[Declaration of Independence](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Declaration-of-Independence) concluded that a world’s fair would be the most appropriate type of celebration. Consequently, the U.S. [Centennial Exhibition](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Centennial-Exposition-worlds-fair-Philadelphia-United-States-1876) was held in [Philadelphia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Philadelphia) in 1876. Its critical success and attendance of just under 10 million were enough to offset a large financial loss, and it inspired a rush of world’s fairs in the United States, especially in the South, over the next 40 years.

[![Image 29: Corliss steam engine](https://cdn.britannica.com/11/71511-050-4FB36986/energy-Corliss-steam-engine-Machinery-Hall-Philadelphia-1876.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/11/71511-050-4FB36986/energy-Corliss-steam-engine-Machinery-Hall-Philadelphia-1876.jpg)

[Corliss steam engine](https://cdn.britannica.com/11/71511-050-4FB36986/energy-Corliss-steam-engine-Machinery-Hall-Philadelphia-1876.jpg)The Corliss steam engine generated all the energy used in Machinery Hall at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, 1876.(more)

The Philadelphia centennial exhibition was particularly noteworthy in showing off the products of the early [Industrial Revolution](https://www.britannica.com/event/Industrial-Revolution) in America. Fairgoers were amazed by the 700-ton Corliss engine, the largest [steam engine](https://www.britannica.com/technology/steam-engine) ever built, and by new inventions such as the [telephone](https://www.britannica.com/technology/telephone), the typewriter, and the mechanical calculator. In addition, the [exposition](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exposition) hosted the first international art exhibition in the United States and was the first to spread exhibits out over several large, topically designated pavilions, a practice that soon became standard. Some 24 states erected their own pavilions as well, an idea repeated at many later fairs.

[![Image 30: 1893 World's Columbian Exposition](https://cdn.britannica.com/05/96805-050-E35DC6CF/view-grounds-buildings-lakefront-Worlds-Columbian-Exposition-1892.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/05/96805-050-E35DC6CF/view-grounds-buildings-lakefront-Worlds-Columbian-Exposition-1892.jpg)

[1893 World's Columbian Exposition](https://cdn.britannica.com/05/96805-050-E35DC6CF/view-grounds-buildings-lakefront-Worlds-Columbian-Exposition-1892.jpg)Bird's-eye view of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago; lithograph by Currier and Ives.(more)

Although there were many important expositions in the last decades of the 19th century, the [World’s Columbian Exposition](https://www.britannica.com/event/Worlds-Columbian-Exposition) in [Chicago](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicago) in 1893 was arguably the most significant world’s fair in U.S. history and one of the most important in the history of world expositions. Coming soon after the spectacular [1889 exposition](https://www.britannica.com/topic/International-Exposition-of-1889) in [Paris](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paris), where the [Eiffel Tower](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Eiffel-Tower-Paris-France) was the main attraction, the World’s Columbian Exposition, in the minds of its organizers, had to be bigger and more important than its Parisian [predecessor](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/predecessor). Chicago’s managers never found a signature structure to surpass the Eiffel Tower (although the [Ferris wheel](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ferris-wheel) did make its debut at the Chicago fair), but they did create an exposition whose architecture shaped the country’s style for the next 25 years and whose exhibits were more impressive than anything seen before. Moreover, the exposition introduced the concept of the midway, a lively entertainment zone, a feature that soon became a staple of virtually all future expositions.

[![Image 32: Postcard image of an international naval display, part of the Jamestown Exhibition held in Norfolk, Virginia, 1907.](https://cdn.britannica.com/08/152608-050-A5AA2476/Postcard-image-part-display-Jamestown-Exhibition-Virginia-1907.jpg?w=300) 2 of 2](https://cdn.britannica.com/08/152608-050-A5AA2476/Postcard-image-part-display-Jamestown-Exhibition-Virginia-1907.jpg)

[Postcard image of an international naval display, part of the Jamestown Exhibition held in Norfolk, Virginia, 1907.](https://cdn.britannica.com/08/152608-050-A5AA2476/Postcard-image-part-display-Jamestown-Exhibition-Virginia-1907.jpg)(more)

The World’s Columbian Exposition marked the peak of the golden age of fairs. It was more spectacular than anything that had preceded it, and, with the possible exception of the great Exposition Universelle (Paris, 1900), no later exposition matched its splendour or its influence. Still, a major international exposition was held almost annually somewhere in the world between 1893 and 1916, when World War I brought a temporary end to the movement. Some, like [St. Louis](https://www.britannica.com/place/Saint-Louis-Missouri#ref235317) (1904) and [San Francisco](https://www.britannica.com/place/San-Francisco-California/The-growth-of-the-metropolis#ref215871) (1915), were large and showy. Others, like the Jamestown Exhibition—held in [Norfolk](https://www.britannica.com/place/Norfolk-Virginia), Virginia (1907), for the 300th anniversary of the [Jamestown Colony](https://www.britannica.com/place/Jamestown-Colony)—were smaller and marked important historical anniversaries. Still others, like London’s Franco-British Exhibition (1908), signified [bilateral](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/bilateral) friendship. In addition, some smaller countries hosted expositions to mark their emergence onto the international scene, such as the Belgian expositions in [Liège](https://www.britannica.com/place/Liege-Belgium) (1905) and [Brussels](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brussels/The-20th-century#ref9681) (1910).

[![Image 33: Postcard image of the U.S. Government Building, Trans-Mississippi and International Exposition, Omaha, Nebraska, 1898.](https://cdn.britannica.com/09/152609-050-FC79E053/Postcard-image-US-Government-Building-Trans-Mississippi-and-1898.jpg?w=300)](https://cdn.britannica.com/09/152609-050-FC79E053/Postcard-image-US-Government-Building-Trans-Mississippi-and-1898.jpg)

[Postcard image of the U.S. Government Building, Trans-Mississippi and International Exposition, Omaha, Nebraska, 1898.](https://cdn.britannica.com/09/152609-050-FC79E053/Postcard-image-US-Government-Building-Trans-Mississippi-and-1898.jpg)(more)

The world’s fairs held in the [United States](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-United-States) during this golden era tended to have characteristic differences from those held in Europe. U.S. participation in European fairs was privately managed. The absence of government involvement carried over to the organization of expositions in the United States, where federal aid was confined to U.S. government pavilions and exhibits. European fairs were, to a far larger extent, government enterprises. Another difference was that American fairs much more readily included entertainment [venues](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/venues) in the form of rides, exotic attractions, and, by the 1890s, so-called foreign or native “villages” that showed fairgoers the way of life of groups from Africa, Asia, and the South Pacific islands, who were generally presented as belonging to, in the parlance of the time, “primitive” societies. By the first decade of the 20th century, fairs in Europe also had adopted these types of entertainment attractions.
